name: Djibouti
headline: Djibouti's 2025 Digital Code gives patients strong rights on paper, but its data commission is not verified as working and records stay in separate systems.

access.summary: The 2025 Digital Code gives a right to a copy within one month, directly or through a chosen doctor, but copies can cost the reproduction price. Public bodies, which run most care, have two years to comply and there is no portal, so 35.
detail: Articles 32 and 33 of the Digital Code (Law 019/AN/23, published 18 September 2025) give a right to know what data is held and to get a copy. A request made electronically gets an electronic answer.
Article 25 sets a one-month deadline, extendable by two months. Article 22 makes rights free in general, but Article 33 lets the controller charge up to the cost of reproduction for a copy.

Article 34 says health data can be accessed by the person directly or through a doctor of their choice. Article 46 adds portability in a machine-readable format for data processed by consent or contract.

Public bodies have two years from entry into force to comply (Article 784). A January 2026 fact sheet said it was unclear whether a data authority had been appointed, and we found no decree naming its members. We found no national portal where patients can see their record.

control.summary: Health data may be processed without consent for care by a professional bound by secrecy, and there is no shared record, opt-out or access log in use. Article 731 makes the national ID number the compulsory health identifier.
detail: Article 62 bans processing of health data, but lifts the ban for diagnosis and care when a health professional bound by secrecy does it. Patient consent is not needed for treatment records.

Article 731 makes the national identification number the health identifier for everyone and says its use is compulsory. Article 755 lets a person object to hosting of their health data, but only for legitimate reasons.

Article 741 says every action in the planned national health data system is logged and the logs are open to the person. That system needs a decree to exist, and we found none, so no patient can use this log today.
The patient's main tool now is the general right to object on grounds tied to their situation (Article 37).

sources.title: Loi n°019/AN/23/9ème L portant Code du Numérique (Journal Officiel, full text PDF)

privacy.summary: The Digital Code bans health data processing outside listed exceptions, requires 72-hour breach notice and allows fines up to DJF 70 million or 5% of turnover. With no health cases and no regulator verified as working, this scores the general law at 45.
detail: Article 14 requires notice to the commission within 72 hours of learning of a breach. Article 15 requires telling the person when the risk is high.

Article 135 allows fines up to DJF 70 million or 5% of worldwide turnover, but not when the State is the controller. Article 145 punishes storing health data without express consent, outside legal cases, with 5 to 10 years in prison.
The commission has 12 members; the President of the Republic names three and also the chair (Articles 106 and 107). Article 131 lets a decree exempt state security files from its checks.

A December 2025 law creating a cybersecurity agency tells it to work with the data commission. We found no enforcement decision and no health breach report. Djibouti is outside the EU, so the EHDS does not apply; Article 99 allows transfers abroad only to countries with equivalent protection.

commercial.summary: Article 736 bans selling health data that can identify a person, even with their consent, with up to 5 years in prison. Electronic marketing needs prior consent, but we found no rules on health apps or de-identified data, and no enforcement.
detail: Article 736 bans any paid transfer of health data that directly or indirectly identifies the person, including with their agreement. The penalty is up to five years in prison and a DJF 4.5 million fine.
Article 514 bans direct marketing by SMS, email or similar means without prior consent. Article 37 lets anyone refuse marketing use of their data at any time, free of charge.
We found no rule on data brokers, consumer health apps or sale of de-identified health data, and no case brought under these articles.

journey.summary: Facilities report to DHIS2 and a pharmacy stock system runs in 32 of the 60 public facilities in a World Bank project, but there is no national electronic record. The main hospital had no patient record system in October 2025 and was still defining one.
detail: The World Bank's October 2025 review lists DHIS2 use in all project facilities. The mSupply pharmacy logistics system ran in 32 of the 60 project facilities, with 48 targeted by project end.
mSupply modules for vaccination and family planning digitise patient-level data in facilities. A 2025 UN article said the family planning record covers 23 public facilities.

A lab information system was planned for 15 pilot sites from January 2026. Whether it started is not verified. The university hospital (CHU) uses TOTALIS and asked for a patient record and radiology system instead of hospital administration software.
The Digital Code plans a national health data system and interoperability rules, both waiting for decrees. WHO said in September 2026 that full digitalisation remains a challenge.

clinical.summary: A clinician can see what is in their own facility's file, but there is no shared record across providers. The main hospital was still choosing a patient record system in late 2025.
detail: Article 62 allows clinicians to process health data for care. There is no national record they can open to see notes from another facility.
In 2024 the Health Ministry said a computerised medical record was used at the Dar El Hanan maternity and that it planned to extend it to all facilities. Progress on that plan is not verified.
Article 772 says telemedicine must give clinicians access to the medical data needed for the act, but this applies only to remote care.

research.summary: Health research on personal data needs prior authorisation from the data commission after an expert committee opinion, and each person must be told and can object. With the commission not verified as working, the opt-out cannot yet be shown to operate, so 50.
detail: Articles 81 and 82 require prior authorisation from the commission, after an advisory committee of research and epidemiology experts gives an opinion within one month.
Article 89 lets anyone object to their data leaving professional secrecy for research. Identifying biological samples and genetic studies need written, express consent.
Article 146 punishes research processing done without informing people, or despite their objection, with 5 to 10 years in prison and DJF 7 to 35 million in fines.
An ethics committee at the National Institute of Public Health gives opinions on research projects (Law 99/AN/10). No public register of authorised uses was found.

ai.summary: Djibouti has no rules for AI in clinical care and no regulation of AI as a medical device. A national AI strategy was presented in September 2026, and the readiness review found no AI law.
detail: UNESCO reported that the digital economy ministry held a consultation in January 2026 on the first national AI strategy, using UNESCO's readiness method.
We Are Tech Africa reported in September 2026 that the readiness review found no dedicated AI law, and rated readiness at about 24.5 out of 100.

Article 65 of the Digital Code bars decisions with legal or significant effects based only on automated processing, except with safeguards that include a right to human intervention. This is a general rule, not a clinical AI rule.

laws.what: Creates the ANC, which must help protect personal data in coordination with the data commission.

laws.what: Sets up universal health insurance run by the CNSS, with medical advisers bound by confidentiality.

news.headline: Digital ministry consults on first national AI strategy with UNESCO and ESCWA
news.why: Health AI has no rules yet; the strategy is the first step toward any.

news.headline: Ministry e-health chief works on digitising medical records and linking data
news.why: Linking ministry, CNSS and military hospital data would affect who sees patient records.

news.headline: Ahead of first national AI forum, AI readiness put at 24.5 out of 100
news.why: Telemedicine is named as an AI use, with no clinical AI safeguards in place.

news.headline: AI strategy presented while review finds no dedicated AI law
news.why: Confirms patients have no specific protection when AI is used in their care.

news.headline: WHO says full digitalisation of the health information system remains a challenge
news.why: Patients' records stay largely on paper and unlinked between facilities.
